about.heading: About me
about.copy:
I am a full-stack developer and founder of ScaleWeb Solutions. I work where business needs and technology meet: turning unclear processes into straightforward tools, or turning a website into a channel that actually supports the business.

My toolkit includes .NET, Angular, Azure, security fundamentals, and SEO. I work from discovery and technical planning through development, launch, and further improvement.

article1.body:
A website has only a few seconds to establish trust. If the page loads slowly, a carefully designed offer may not matter because some visitors leave before they see it. Speed is therefore more than a technical detail. It affects the first impression, how easily people absorb the content, and how many visits continue toward an inquiry or purchase.

The difference is particularly clear on mobile. A visitor may have a limited connection, use an older phone, or be in the middle of another task. Heavy images, unnecessary scripts, and distracting animations make every step feel slower. A strong solution begins with priorities: compress images, load only what is needed, keep the code straightforward, and place the most important content early. Clear headings and an obvious next action matter just as much as raw loading time.

Performance also influences search visibility. Google considers user experience, but a fast page cannot compensate for unclear content. Technology, messaging, and structure have to work together. Do not rely on a single laboratory score. Observe how real visitors use the site, where they leave, and which devices they use.

The most profitable improvement is often not a complete rebuild. Resizing images, removing third-party code, simplifying navigation, and clarifying the path to contact may be enough. The result is a website that feels reliable, responds immediately, and helps the customer move forward. Like a good salesperson, it respects the visitor's time and makes the next step easy.
article2.body:
Excel is an excellent tool for testing an idea, making calculations, and collecting information quickly. Trouble begins when a temporary spreadsheet becomes the company's central system. Multiple copies start circulating, formulas are changed accidentally, and nobody knows which version is current. Employees spend time moving information between email, documents, and tabs instead of working on the business itself.

Several warning signs tend to appear. The same details are entered in multiple places. Only one person understands how the file works. It is difficult to see who changed what, and reports require manual assembly every week or month. As the business grows, the sheet becomes slower while the consequences of an error increase. The bottleneck is not Excel itself, but a workflow without clear rules or a shared data source.

A custom digital tool does not need to replace everything at once. Start with the part that consumes the most time or causes the most errors. Map which roles use the information, which steps require approval, and what data already exists in other systems. A focused web interface can then bring registration, validation, status, and reporting into one place. Automated reminders and integrations can be added once the core workflow is sound.

The aim is not to reproduce every old routine exactly as it is. It is to simplify the work. A good solution reduces duplicate entry, makes responsibility visible, and gives the right person the right information at the right time. Excel can remain useful for analysis and exports without carrying the entire process. Technology then supports growth instead of slowing it down.
article3.body:
A sustainable web solution rarely begins with a framework choice. It begins with a clear view of the problem: who will use the solution, what work should become easier, and what does success look like? A requirement such as “we need a customer portal” reveals very little. A stronger goal might be that customers can check order status themselves and support receives fewer repetitive questions.

Once the goal is clear, the right features can be prioritized. Every request does not need to enter the first release. The smallest useful version should cover one complete flow from beginning to end so it can be tested in reality. Feedback from real users is more valuable than assumptions in a long requirements document. It reveals which steps are unclear, what information is missing, and what genuinely saves time.

Technical choices should then support the need. A simple web application may be better than a complex microservice architecture when the team is small and demand is predictable. The foundation should still provide secure sign-in, validated data, backups, logging, and clear permissions. These qualities keep the solution manageable as more users, integrations, and business rules are introduced.

Sustainability also depends on ownership. The code should be understandable, the operating environment documented, and important dependencies updateable without drama. Measure the result with business-oriented indicators such as shorter handling time, fewer errors, better data quality, or happier customers. When every major technical choice connects to such an outcome, it becomes easier to decide what to build now, what can wait, and when the solution needs to evolve.
